program_meta.advisor_model: ADVISOR-MATCHED, NOT DEPARTMENT ADMISSION - and the mechanism is stated with unusual precision by Waterloo itself. The 'Applying and admissions' page, VERBATIM, under 'Determine a research area': 'Look into our 15 research areas and the faculty members working within them. Determine which supervisors you'd be interested in working with - we will ask for a list of them on your application. Remember: You do not need a supervisor to apply, but you do need one to be accepted!' Separately, the MMath CS program page, VERBATIM, under 'Supervisors': 'It is not required to find a supervisor before applying. However, students are advised to establish contact with potential supervisors before applying.' MECHANISM, explained: (1) the application form itself asks the applicant to LIST prospective supervisors (this is a required field, not optional colour commentary in the SOP); (2) admission decisions are not made purely by a department committee - a named faculty member must be willing to take the student on, i.e. acceptance is contingent on a faculty match, functionally similar to how PhD admission works at many US research universities, NOT like Purdue's department-first, advisor-after-arrival model; (3) 'establishing contact... before applying' is explicitly advised, meaning the pre-application email that is optional-but-helpful at Purdue is closer to load-bearing at Waterloo - a cold, contact-free application with a plausible-sounding supervisor list is weaker than one where a supervisor already knows the applicant's name. STRATEGY IMPLICATION: Akshat should not submit this application without having emailed and ideally received some signal of interest from at least one named supervisor; the SOP's 'faculty of interest' list is not decorative, it is functionally the routing mechanism for who reviews the file.
program_meta.ms_research_access: Yes - MMath is inherently a supervised research degree once admission is only offered on the thesis track, and the whole admissions model (see advisor_model) is built around the student joining a specific supervisor's group from day one, not TAing broadly and picking a lab later as at some department-admission schools.

faculty.research_areas: Generative models, convex and nonconvex optimization, trustworthy machine learning, robustness (including data poisoning), applications in computer vision and NLP.
faculty.why_match: Yu's 2025-2026 output is squarely on the generative-model / data-quality axis Akshat works in. 'Stochastic Forward-Backward Deconvolution: Training Diffusion Models with Finite Noisy Datasets' (ICML 2025) is a direct methodological neighbour of Akshat's DDPM-pretraining-on-unlabelled-abdominal-CT result - both ask how much a diffusion model can learn from a small, imperfect unlabelled corpus, and Akshat's unresolved negative result (frozen encoder beats fine-tuned on liver but falls below random init on kidney) is exactly the kind of failure mode this line of work is built to explain. 'Exploring the Limits of Model-Targeted Indiscriminate Data Poisoning Attacks' (ICML 2023, with Gautam Kamath) treats the training SET itself as the attack surface, which is the adversarial mirror of Akshat's A-PDF filter - a post-hoc plausibility check on GAN-generated pseudo-images meant to keep bad synthetic data out of training, i.e. the defensive version of the same question.

faculty.research_areas: Probabilistic and Bayesian machine learning (sum-product networks, Bayesian moment matching), reinforcement learning and POMDPs, uncertainty quantification and calibration, federated learning, generative models for text/image, constrained/inverse RL.
faculty.why_match: Two directly relevant 2024 papers anchor the uncertainty-quantification overlap with interest (B): 'Preventing Arbitrarily High Confidence on Far-Away Data in Point-Estimated Discriminative Neural Networks' (AISTATS 2024) attacks the same problem Akshat's confidence-thresholding pseudo-label filter runs into in practice - a discriminative network can be badly overconfident on out-of-distribution inputs, which is precisely why he added MC-dropout uncertainty as a second filtering signal rather than trusting softmax confidence alone. 'Calibrated One Round Federated Learning with Bayesian Inference in the Predictive Space' (AAAI 2024) and the broader sum-product-network line treat probabilistic calibration as a first-class architectural concern, the same posture HiME takes toward hierarchy consistency (built in, not corrected post hoc). The fit is real but narrower than it first looks: his current output (2024-2026) is dominated by reinforcement learning, multi-agent systems, and LLM-adjacent work (reward-guided text generation, LLM agents), not medical imaging or segmentation.
faculty.key_paper_1: Preventing Arbitrarily High Confidence on Far-Away Data in Point-Estimated Discriminative Neural Networks. AISTATS, 2024.
faculty.key_paper_2: Calibrated One Round Federated Learning with Bayesian Inference in the Predictive Space. AAAI, 2024. (See also: Batchnorm with entropic regularization turns deterministic autoencoders into generative models, UAI 2020; Deep Homogeneous Mixture Models: Representation, Separation and Approximation, NeurIPS 2018, with Yaoliang Yu.)

faculty.department: David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science; also Vector Institute for AI
faculty.research_areas: Trustworthy and adversarially robust machine learning, AI security, inference acceleration for LLMs (EAGLE speculative decoding series), world models, learning theory.
faculty.why_match: Zhang's TRADES line ('Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy', ICML 2019 - a top-10 most-influential ICML paper 2019-2024) formalizes exactly the tension Akshat's polyp-segmentation ablation surfaces empirically: a data-side or regularization intervention buys a fixed amount of performance, and that amount shrinks as the model's own capacity/robustness improves (Akshat's preprocessing gain fell from +0.058 Dice on U-Net to +0.023 on Attention U-Net) - both are studying where a cheap intervention stops adding value once the underlying model is already strong. The 'World Models' thread (The Matrix, NeurIPS 2025) is a distant echo of Akshat's generative-pretraining-for-transfer work (DDPM encoder pretraining), though applied to video-game world generation rather than medical imaging.
faculty.key_paper_1: Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy (TRADES). ICML, 2019 (Long Talk).
faculty.key_paper_2: EAGLE-3: Scaling up Inference Acceleration of Large Language Models via Training-Time Test. NeurIPS, 2025. (See also: The Matrix: Infinite-Horizon World Generation with Real-Time Moving Control, NeurIPS 2025.)
faculty.taking_students: Unstated explicitly (no prospective-student notice found), but clearly an extremely active, well-funded, high-visibility group (multiple 2025-2026 NeurIPS/ICML/CVPR papers, Senior Area Chair roles at NeurIPS/ICML 2026, Google Research Scholar Award 2025, Amazon Research Award 2023). Extremely high-profile, extremely active group; likely to be competitive to join.
